catalogue.system: Predator vs prey biomass, and community production vs biomass, across ecosystems
catalogue.law: Predator biomass ∝ (prey biomass)^k, k about 3/4; community production ∝ biomass^about 3/4
catalogue.variable: prey biomass density B (kg/km²) across communities
catalogue.reported: Hatton et al. 2015 (2,260 communities of mammals, invertebrates, plants and plankton): predator–prey and production–biomass exponents are often near 3/4 (press reports about 0.75). Body size does not explain it, and the pattern appears only at whole-community level.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). From memory: Hatton et al. 2015 report predator ∝ prey^~0.75 and production ∝ biomass^~0.75 across about 2,000+ communities in many biomes. I did not retrieve per-biome intervals. Hatton et al. 2019 (PNAS) extend the 3/4 to growth across eukaryotes.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: community production, a flux. Units: units of prey biomass. Denser communities give each unit of biomass a smaller share of production (∝ B^-1/4). Predators live on that production, so they scale as production. No individual-level resource has been identified.
catalogue.best_reading: Predator biomass is discretely orthopolic in prey PRODUCTION (a flux): a constant predator stock per unit prey production across ecosystems. This explains one 3/4 by the other, and the motivation (predators live on production) came first. The value 3/4 itself (production ∝ biomass^0.75 at community level, a density-dependence law with no single organism) has no resource reading. The network analogy is numerology.
catalogue.algebra_note: Under constant transfer efficiency and constant predator turnover, k_pred = k_prod. Production per unit prey biomass ∝ B^-1/4 follows. Consistent.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Moderate for the link: both exponents come from the same ecosystems, and there is no independent production measurement. Very high for any explanation of the value 3/4, which matches Kleiber with no shared network. Social-insect colonies give a similar 3/4 without a network (Hou et al. 2010; Waters et al. 2010). This case is a counterexample to treating 3/4 as a signature of network geometry.

proposed_readings.resource: Predator biomass ∝ prey production (an identity), with production ∝ B^3/4
proposed_readings.composition: k_pred = k_prod when transfer efficiency and predator turnover do not depend on B
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Across the same ecosystems, the production–biomass exponent should predict the predator–prey exponent system by system. Where prey turnover is changed (harvest, enrichment), both exponents should shift together.

proposed_readings.resource: Organism-like supply network, Kleiber transferred to communities (3/(3+1))
proposed_readings.composition: Community production ∝ B^(D/(D+1)) with D = 3
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: If network geometry were the cause, two-dimensional communities (benthic films) and three-dimensional ones (pelagic) should differ (2/3 vs 3/4).

catalogue.system: Branching transport networks: mammalian arterial trees and tree branches
catalogue.law: r0^Δ = Σ ri^Δ at each bifurcation (Murray Δ = 3; Leonardo Δ = 2). For a self-similar tree, vessels per level N ∝ r^-Δ.
catalogue.variable: vessel or branch radius r
catalogue.reported: Murray 1926: Δ = 3 (laminar, minimum work). Turbulent: Δ = 7/3 (Uylings 1977, via secondary sources). Measured: small arteries 2.7-3.0; cat and chick arteries 2.49-2.59; coronary meta-analysis 2.39 (95% CI 2.24-2.54, I² = 99%); human pulmonary 2.31 ± 0.60. Trees: Leonardo Δ ≈ 2, with 1.8 < Δ < 2.3 for many species (Eloy 2011).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Measured Δ: about 3 in small vessels, 2.3-2.6 in large and coronary arteries, and 1.8-2.3 in tree branches (Eloy 2011, as I recall). α = Δ + 1 is therefore 3.3-4 for arteries and 2.8-3.3 for trees. Using a single 3.7 for arteries hides a systematic crossover, not noise. I could not check the coronary meta-analysis value (2.39) or the pulmonary value.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: volumetric flow Q, a flux. Every level carries all the blood (mass conservation), so total flow per level, i.e. per log-radius step, is constant. The network is therefore exactly log-orthopolic in flow per vessel q(r) ∝ r^Δ. The content lies in the flow–radius law q ∝ r^Δ, which a cost optimization fixes. For trees the conserved quantity is cross-sectional area (pipe model) or bending stress.
catalogue.best_reading: Volumetric flow per vessel, log measure. Each generation carries the full flow, and q ∝ r^3 follows from laminar minimum work (Murray), which fits small vessels where Δ ≈ 3. For coronary arteries (Δ ≈ 2.3-2.45), crediting the turbulent 7/3 is unjustified: coronary flow is laminar (Re of order 10^2). Huo & Kassab 2012 derive Q ∝ D^(7/3) for coronary trees from a laminar volume-length model (from memory), a different mechanism giving the same number. For tree branches, three derivations (pipe model, elastic similarity, Eloy's wind stress) all give Δ = 2 while naming different resources.
catalogue.algebra_note:
I checked each step:
- Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a) from minimizing dissipation plus upkeep.
- Poiseuille (a = 2, c = 4) gives 3.
- Rough turbulence (a = 3, c = 5) gives 7/3.
- Blasius (a = 11/4, c = 19/4) gives 27/11 ≈ 2.45.
- A self-similar tree has N_k ∝ r_k^-Δ, evenly spaced in ln r, so α = Δ + 1.
Log-orthopolity in flow is an IDENTITY: mass conservation makes every generation carry the whole flow. All the content lies in the per-vessel law q ∝ r^Δ.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for laminar Δ = 3, which was derived in 1926 before the measurements. High for the 2.3-2.5 regime, where the turbulent and Huo-Kassab readings fit equally and turbulence is physically absent. For trees the exponent is robust but cannot select a resource (hydraulic pipes, cross-section or section modulus). Because the orthopolity here holds by construction, the case cannot test the program.

proposed_readings.resource: Flow per vessel under laminar minimum work (Murray's law)
proposed_readings.composition: Minimize dissipation (∝ Q^a r^-c) plus blood-volume upkeep (∝ r^2), giving Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a). Poiseuille flow has a = 2 and c = 4, so Δ = (4+2)/2 = 3.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Δ should fall as Reynolds number rises in larger vessels. The same reading, linear-orthopolic in hydraulic conductance ∝ r^4 (α = 4), is algebraically the same statement and not independent evidence.

proposed_readings.resource: Flow per vessel under turbulent minimum work
proposed_readings.composition: Fully rough turbulence: ΔP ∝ Q^2 r^-5, so power ∝ Q^3 r^-5 (a = 3, c = 5) and Δ = (5+2)/3 = 7/3. Blasius smooth turbulence gives (19/4 + 2)/(11/4) = 27/11 ≈ 2.45 (my calculation).
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Within one arterial tree, Δ should move from about 2.3-2.45 near the aorta to 3 in arterioles, crossing over at a definite Reynolds number. Microcirculation deviates because of the Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect.

proposed_readings.resource: Cross-sectional area (Leonardo; pipe model; uniform wind stress)
proposed_readings.composition: Area ∝ r^2: two transverse dimensions. In the pipe model each leaf is served by a pipe of fixed cross-section, so the number of pipes ∝ r^2.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Trees in sheltered understoreys, or with non-self-similar architecture, should deviate. In arteries, WBE predict area preservation (Δ = 2) in large pulsatile vessels and Δ = 3 in small ones, crossing where the Womersley number is about 1.

catalogue.system: Lévy-flight foraging step lengths (marine predators, insects, birds, mammals)
catalogue.law: P(l) ∝ l^-μ for move-step lengths, μ ≈ 2 ('inverse-square Lévy walk')
catalogue.variable: move-step length l (m or km), or flight duration
catalogue.reported: Viswanathan et al. 1999: μ = 2 is optimal for sparse, revisitable targets, and data on insects, mammals and birds were consistent with it. Edwards et al. 2007: the albatross, deer and bumblebee Lévy claims are not supported (albatross flights are gamma-distributed). Sims et al. 2008: sharks, bony fishes, turtles and penguins show Lévy-like movement near the theoretical optimum (one basking shark has μ ≈ 2.3). Humphries et al. 2010: Lévy movement in low-productivity waters, Brownian in productive ones. Levernier et al. 2020: μ = 2 is not optimal in two or more dimensions.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Where a Lévy model is preferred, μ ≈ 1.6-2.6 (Sims et al. 2008; Humphries et al. 2010). Many datasets prefer exponential, gamma or composite Brownian models (Edwards et al. 2007). Pyke 2015 argues the Lévy foraging hypothesis should be abandoned.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the forager's travel budget (distance, or time at constant speed). Units: steps, sized by step length. The walk is log-orthopolic in distance: the total distance covered in steps of each log-length class is the same, so no search scale is favoured. This is a flux or time-budget reading.
catalogue.best_reading: Travel effort (distance or time) spread equally over log step-length classes (log measure): no search scale is favoured. The catalogue missed a theory that gives exactly this reading. Guinard & Korman 2021 (Sci Adv, from memory) show that intermittent inverse-square walks are near-optimal at once for targets of ALL sizes in 2D, i.e. equal effort per scale under scale ignorance. This rescues μ = 2 after Levernier et al. 2020 showed it is not optimal for a fixed target size in d ≥ 2. The data are weak: Lévy fits are contested, and foragers switch to Brownian movement where prey are dense (Humphries et al. 2010).
catalogue.algebra_note: d_log = μ - 1 = 1: total distance per log length class, l·l^-2·l, is constant. d_lin = 2. Both correct.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. Composite correlated random walks (mixtures of exponentials; Benhamou 2007) mimic μ ≈ 2 over 1-2 decades. Fits are sensitive to the method (Edwards et al. 2007). Density-dependent switching contradicts universal scale-free effort, which is the reading's own prediction.

proposed_readings.resource: Travel distance (time) per step ∝ l, equal per log scale
proposed_readings.composition: Equal effort per log scale: n_log(l) × l = constant
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: The equal-effort reading predicts μ = 2 regardless of prey density and dimension. Search optimization instead predicts Brownian movement (μ → 3) where prey are abundant, and μ → 1 for destructive foraging. Humphries et al. observed density-dependent switching, which favours optimization over equal effort.

proposed_readings.resource: Steps allocated in proportion to gaps in the prey field
proposed_readings.composition: μ_move = μ_gap: the walk reproduces the distribution of distances between prey patches
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: μ_move equals the prey-gap exponent measured in the same habitat
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Measure prey-gap and movement exponents in the same habitat: the reading predicts equality, with movement exponents shifting between habitats in step with prey statistics.

catalogue.system: Word tokens in written texts and corpora (English; Moby Dick; Google Books)
catalogue.law: Zipf: frequency of the r-th most common word f(r) ∝ r^-γ with γ ≈ 1. Equivalently, the number of word types with k occurrences is dN/dk ∝ k^-α, with α ≈ 2.
catalogue.variable: k = occurrences (tokens) of a word type in the text (dimensionless count)
catalogue.reported: Rank exponent γ ≈ 1 for frequent words (the 'kernel lexicon'). In large corpora, rare words have γ ≈ 2 (Ferrer i Cancho & Solé 2001, abstract; two regimes confirmed in Google Books by Petersen et al. 2012). For Moby Dick the MLE density exponent is α = 1.95 at x_min = 7 (Clauset et al. 2009, confirmed via the poweRlaw documentation and arXiv 2311.11200). Newman 2005 gets α = 2.20 for the same text with x_min = 1.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Clauset et al. 2009 give 1.95 ± 0.02 at x_min = 7 ± 2 (18,855 types). Newman 2005 gives 2.20 ± 0.01 at x_min = 1. The kernel lexicon has rank exponent ≈ 1. In large corpora the rare-word regime has rank exponent ≈ 2, i.e. density ≈ 1.5. Confirmed from my recollection of the primary sources and from docs/zeta-compilation.md. Web tools did not work in this task: the search budget was exhausted, WebFetch failed on DNS, and the proxy blocked arXiv.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the N tokens of the text. Units: word types. Resource per unit: the type's token count. This is a stock within a fixed text and a usage flux in a growing corpus. d_log ≈ 1 means the resource is the token count itself: each factor-of-ten band of word frequency carries about the same share of the running text. In large corpora the rare-word regime has d_log ≈ 0.5 while the kernel regime keeps d_log ≈ 1. The linear reading (d_lin ≈ 2) makes the text linear-orthopolic in k², the number of same-type token pairs (coincidences).
catalogue.best_reading: The tokens themselves (q = k), under the log measure. Resource is fixed by definition, so nothing was chosen to fit: d_log ≈ 1 means each factor-of-ten frequency band carries about the same token mass. The mechanism is Simon/Yule reuse with innovation. Equivalently, types enter at a steady rate, so relative age t/t_i is exactly log-orthopolic (P(u) > u = 1/u), and counts grow as (t/t_i)^(1−a), giving ζ = 1/(1−a).
catalogue.algebra_note: α = 1 + 1/γ, d_log = 0.95 and d_lin = 1.95 are correct. Simon's ζ = 1/(1−a) = 1.09–1.11 for a = 0.08–0.10 (recomputed). However, Simon's model forces α > 2 for any a > 0. The x_min = 7 fit (1.95 ± 0.02) lies below 2, and the prediction (2.1) sits between two fits that each have small stated errors: 7σ from one and 5σ from the other. 'Matches within error' holds only if the x_min systematic is counted as the error. The pairs reading is just the identity d_lin = d_log + 1.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for d_log ≈ 1 with q = k, because nothing is adjustable and the motivation (Zipf, Simon 1955) is genuinely prior. High for the correction a/(1−a) ≈ 0.1: it is smaller than the x_min systematic (ζ = 0.95–1.20), so it is untested. Simon also predicts linear vocabulary growth, which Heaps' law contradicts. The least-effort reading stays suggestive, since it needs tuning to a critical point. The coincidence-pairs reading is numerology, as the catalogue says.

proposed_readings.resource: Tokens (k itself), under proportional reuse with innovation
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 (tokens) + a/(1−a) (innovation share). In Simon's model, each new token is a new word with probability a; otherwise it repeats an existing word chosen in proportion to that word's count. Log-frequency therefore grows at a rate independent of frequency, and the token flux is conserved (transport identity B = F/v with constant v).
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: ζ = 1/(1−a). For Moby Dick, a = types/tokens ≈ (17,000–21,000)/(208,000–215,000) ≈ 0.08–0.10 (tokenization-dependent counts found in this task), so ζ ≈ 1.09–1.11 and α ≈ 2.1.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: ζ − 1 ≈ a. Across many texts, with x_min fixed in advance, fitted ζ − 1 should track the type/token ratio V/N. An innovation rate that falls with N (Heaps) predicts a second, steeper-in-rank regime for rare words, and that regime is observed (γ ≈ 2).

proposed_readings.resource: Balance of speaker and hearer effort (least effort)
proposed_readings.composition: No resource product. In Ferrer i Cancho & Solé's (2003) signal–object optimization, an exponent near 1 appears only at a critical value λ* of the weight given to speaker versus hearer cost.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: Rank exponent ≈ 1 at λ*; no power law elsewhere
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Because the exponent needs tuning to λ*, systems away from the transition should lose the power law rather than shift its exponent.

proposed_readings.resource: Same-type token pairs k(k−1)/2 (coincidences)
proposed_readings.composition: k² = k × k: tokens times the frequency of the same word
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: None independent of the token reading, from which it cannot be distinguished.

catalogue.system: Vocabulary growth in texts and corpora (English corpora; Reuters RCV1; novels; Google Books)
catalogue.law: Heaps' law: V(N) ∝ N^β, where V is the number of distinct word types after N tokens
catalogue.variable: N = tokens read (text length); V = distinct types
catalogue.reported: β ≈ 0.4–0.6 for English corpora (encyclopedia summary). b = 0.49 for Reuters RCV1 (information-retrieval lecture fit). β ≈ 0.78 for individual English novels (review of statistical laws, arXiv 2407.19874). β → 1 at the start of a text. Large corpora show two regimes (Gerlach & Altmann 2013; Petersen et al. 2012, 'decreasing need for new words').
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: β ≈ 0.4–0.6 for English corpora. RCV1 gives b = 0.49 with k ≈ 44 (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, IR textbook; recollection). Single texts and early growth give higher values, about 0.7–1. The implied rare-tail density exponent is α = 1 + β ≈ 1.4–1.6. The catalogue's alpha_density field holds β = 0.5, which is not a density exponent; I report 1.5. The 0.78 value for novels (arXiv 2407.19874) was not verified.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the N tokens. Units: word types. V(N) counts the types whose probability exceeds roughly 1/N, so V(N) is the survival function of type probabilities read at threshold 1/N, and β is the survival exponent ζ of the rare-word tail. Mean tokens per type, N/V ∝ N^(1−β), keeps growing: the text's budget is spread over a vocabulary that grows sublinearly. In resource terms, ζ = 0.5 means token mass per log-frequency band rises as p^0.5 inside the rare-word regime. That is top-heavy: the frequent (kernel) words hold most tokens. Vocabulary is a count of discovered slots (a capacity), not a stock.
catalogue.best_reading: Heaps' law has no resource of its own. It is the sampling transform of the rare-word Zipf tail: V(N) counts the types with p ≳ 1/N, so β = ζ_rare. Its orthopolic content is the rare-word tail, where token mass per log-frequency band rises as p^0.5 (top-heavy). This is a derived identity (Mandelbrot; Lü, Zhang & Zhou 2010).
catalogue.algebra_note: This is an error in one field only. d_log = 0.5 and d_lin = 1.5 are correct for the implied rare-word tail (ζ = β, α = 1.5). As recorded, though, alpha_density = 0.5 makes d_log = α − 1 fail; set it to 1.5 or N/A. β = 1/γ holds only for γ > 1; for γ ≤ 1, β → 1 (V ∝ N/ln N at γ = 1). The reading N/V ∝ N^(1−β) is consistent. The type-pairs model dV/dN ∝ 1/V gives V ∝ N^(1/2) correctly, but nothing motivates it.
catalogue.numerology_risk: The identity has no free parameter. It is only approximate in real texts: topical burstiness makes vocabulary grow more slowly than in a shuffled text, so β and ζ_rare must be fitted on the same corpus with x_min set in advance. The V² ∝ N type-pairs reading is numerology. Because ζ_rare ≈ 0.5 < 1, a stock (tokens) can be top-heavy, which contradicts the catalogue's own 'stocks sit at d_log ≥ 1' regularity.

proposed_readings.resource: Token mass per log-frequency band of the rare-word tail, inherited from Zipf
proposed_readings.composition: β = ζ_rare = 1/γ_rare. The rare-word regime has γ ≈ 2, so β ≈ 1/2.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: On the same corpus, β must equal the ζ fitted to the rare-word tail. Short texts dominated by the kernel regime (γ ≈ 1) must show β → 1 with a log correction (V ∝ N/ln N). This is consistent with β ≈ 0.78 for single novels and β → 1 early in a text.

proposed_readings.resource: Pairs of distinct types
proposed_readings.composition: If each new type arrives at a rate inversely proportional to the vocabulary already used, dV/dN ∝ 1/V, then V² ∝ N: tokens are linear-orthopolic in type pairs.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Predicts β = 1/2 for every language in the noncore regime. Language-dependent β, which Gerlach & Altmann report through language-specific parameters, argues against it.

catalogue.system: US metropolitan areas (135 largest MSAs, 1991) and 'natural' cities built by clustering populated cells (USA, Great Britain)
catalogue.law: P(S > s) ∝ s^-ζ (rank-size: ln rank = c − ζ ln s), with ζ ≈ 1
catalogue.variable: s = city population (persons)
catalogue.reported: ζ = 1.005 from OLS rank-size on 135 MSAs, R² = 0.986 (Gabaix 1999, via MIT lecture notes). Gabaix notes an OLS bias of about 0.05 and a true SE of about 0.1. The 135 largest US urban areas in 2010 give 1.019. Natural cities: ζ close to 1 down to 12,000 inhabitants (US) and 5,000 (GB) (Rozenfeld et al. 2011). Administrative US places give ζ ≈ 1.3–1.4 (repo compilation, not re-verified here).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: The OLS rank-size fit gives ζ = 1.005 with reported SE 0.010 and R² = 0.986 (135 MSAs, 1991). The correct SE is about ζ√(2/n) ≈ 0.12 (Gabaix & Ibragimov 2011). Administrative US places give α = 2.37 ± 0.08 (Clauset 2009) or 2.30 (Newman 2005), i.e. ζ ≈ 1.3–1.4. Dispersion across countries is large: Soo (2005) rejects Zipf by OLS in 53 of 73 countries.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the national urban population. Units: cities. Resource per unit: residents (a stock). d_log ≈ 1 means residents themselves are the log-orthopolic resource: each factor-of-ten band of city size holds about the same number of people. The linear reading (d_lin ≈ 2) is resident pairs s²/2, the potential within-city contacts per unit of population.
catalogue.best_reading: Residents (q = k) under the log measure, with Gibrat growth and a lower barrier or entry. Gabaix (1999) derives ζ → 1 when s_min/s̄ → 0: people are conserved as cities move up the log-size axis.
catalogue.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 and d_log = 1.005 are correct. Gabaix's ζ = 1/(1 − s_min/s̄) is correct. ζ_A = ζ_P/c under a deterministic A ∝ P^c is correct.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for the resident reading, because the resource is fixed by definition. The resident-pairs reading is numerology. Caveats: the statement concerns a defined upper tail of agglomerations. Over all places the distribution is lognormal (Eeckhout 2004), and ζ depends on how a city is defined. The catalogue's area-versus-Bettencourt test is weak. Rozenfeld's natural-city area is built from populated cells, so area ∝ population is partly true by construction. Built-up land from satellite data would be a cleaner test.

proposed_readings.resource: Residents under proportional (Gibrat) growth with entry and a lower barrier
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 + (ζ − 1), where ζ − 1 ≈ (population entering through new cities as a share of the total) / (resource-weighted log growth rate). The correction tends to 0 when entry is small and the floor is far below the mean (Gabaix: ζ = 1/(1 − s_min/s̄)).
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: ζ depends on how a city is defined: administrative fragmentation steepens the tail to about 1.4, while clustering gives about 1. If area were a deterministic power of population, A ∝ P^c, then ζ_A = ζ_P/c. Rozenfeld et al. report ζ_A ≈ 1 as well, which implies c ≈ 1. This conflicts with the land-area exponent 2/3 of Bettencourt's (2013) framework, which would give ζ_A = 1.5. The tension is a direct test of either the deterministic map or that exponent.

proposed_readings.resource: Resident pairs (potential interactions)
proposed_readings.composition: s² = s × s
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: None beyond the resident reading

catalogue.system: Urban systems: US metropolitan statistical areas and other national urban systems
catalogue.law: Y = Y0 N^β. Socioeconomic outputs: β ≈ 1.15 (GDP), 1.12 (wages), 1.27 (new patents), 1.25 (inventors). Infrastructure: 0.87 (electrical cable length), 0.83 (road surface), 0.77 (gasoline stations). Individual needs (housing, employment, household electricity): ≈ 1.
catalogue.variable: N = metropolitan population; Y = annual output (flux) or infrastructure stock
catalogue.reported: Bettencourt et al. 2007 PNAS. Patents 1.27, inventors 1.25, GDP 1.15, wages 1.12 and cables 0.87 come from the table as reproduced in arXiv 0809.4994; roads 0.83 and gasoline stations 0.77 from a secondary summary. Theory gives 1 ± δ with δ = H/(D(D+H)) = 1/6 for D = 2, H = 1, i.e. 7/6 and 5/6 (Bettencourt 2013; formula verified via a 2016 European urban-scaling paper). Exponents depend on how cities are defined: most England & Wales indicators scale linearly (Arcaute et al. 2015), and many exponents are compatible with 1 once fluctuations are modelled (Leitão et al. 2016).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: The exponents are right, but several are attributed to the wrong country. In Bettencourt et al. 2007, Table 1 (recollection): GDP 1.15 [1.06, 1.23] is China 2002. The same table gives GDP 1.26 for the EU and 1.13 [1.03, 1.23] for Germany 2003. Wages 1.12 (USA 2002), patents 1.27, inventors 1.25 and private R&D employment 1.34 are US values. All the infrastructure values are Germany 2001–2002, not US: cables 0.87 [0.82, 0.92], road surface 0.83 [0.74, 0.92], gasoline stations 0.77, gasoline sales 0.79. Later work puts US MSA GDP at about 1.13.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the city's socioeconomic output Y (a flux per year), or its network area (a stock). Units: residents. Resource per resident: y = Y/N ∝ N^δ with δ ≈ 0.15, so each resident's share grows with city size, while network per resident falls as N^(−δ). In Bettencourt's theory Y ∝ N²/A_n. The final resource is then the number of potential pairs N², divided between output and network, so that Y·A_n ∝ N². The log/linear measure distinction does not apply to a deterministic law; d_log and d_lin here both give the exponent of output in population.
catalogue.best_reading: Output per resident equals social interactions per resident, so d = 1 + δ with δ = H/(D(D+H)). The final resource is the N² potential pairs, shared between output and network area: Y·A_n ∝ N².
catalogue.algebra_note: ζ_Y = ζ_N/β is correct for a deterministic map. δ = H/(D(D+H)) gives 1/6 (D = 2), 1/2 (D = 1) and 1/12 (D = 3); all correct. Y·A_n ∝ N² is an exact rearrangement of Y = G·N²/A_n. The catalogue's sum-rule check ('US values give 1.98–1.99'), however, pairs Chinese GDP or US wages with German infrastructure. Within Germany alone: GDP 1.13 + roads 0.83 = 1.96 and GDP 1.13 + cables 0.87 = 2.00, each with CIs of about ±0.1. The sum rule is consistent but only weakly tested.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Medium. The theory came before the data and gives exactly this reading, but H = 1 is assumed rather than measured. Patents and R&D (1.25–1.34) and gasoline stations (0.77) fall outside 7/6 and 5/6. The exponents shift with how cities are defined (Arcaute et al. 2015; Leitão et al. 2016; Cottineau et al. 2017). The sum rule is an identity of the model. It tests the model only when output and network are measured for the same cities with the same boundaries. I downgraded the grade from 'derived' for these reasons.

proposed_readings.resource: Social interactions per resident = area swept per person (fixed by bounded daily effort) × population density on the network
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 (residents) + δ, with δ = H/(D(D+H)) = (1/D)·(H/(D+H)). D = 2 (the urban plane) and H = 1 (fractal dimension of individual paths) give δ = 1/6.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Dimension dependence with H = 1: D = 1 (ribbon or linear cities) gives δ = 1/2 and β = 1.5; D = 3 gives δ = 1/12 and β ≈ 1.08. Within one urban system, GDP across cities should have a survival exponent ζ ≈ 1/1.15 ≈ 0.87 if populations are Zipf.

proposed_readings.resource: Potential pairs N², shared between socioeconomic output and network area
proposed_readings.composition: Y × A_n ∝ N², so β_Y + β_network = 2 for any δ (my rearrangement of Y = G N²/A_n)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Parameter-free: across urban systems or city definitions (e.g. Arcaute-style boundary ensembles), any shift in the network exponent must be mirrored by an opposite shift in the output exponent.

catalogue.system: US firms with employees (about 5.5 million tax-paying firms, Census 1997)
catalogue.law: P(S > s) ∝ s^-ζ with ζ ≈ 1 (Zipf)
catalogue.variable: s = employees per firm
catalogue.reported: ζ = 1.059, with density slope 2.059, fitted on power-of-three bins over nearly six decades (Axtell 2001 Science, verified via arXiv cond-mat/0401053 and secondary sources). Receipts ζ ≈ 0.99 and 2011 SBA data ζ = 1.097 ± 0.002 come from the repo compilation (not re-verified here).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: ζ = 1.059 (s.e. 0.054, adjusted R² 0.992) from a log-binned fit to 1997 Census data. Receipts give ζ ≈ 0.99 (s.e. ≈ 0.06) in the same paper (recollection). The 2011 SBA binned MLE, 1.097 ± 0.002, comes from the repo compilation.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: private-sector employment. Units: firms. Resource per unit: workers (a stock). d_log ≈ 1.06 means employment per log size band is almost equal and slightly bottom-heavy: small and medium firms hold a little more employment per band than the largest. The linear reading is worker pairs.
catalogue.best_reading: Workers (q = k) under the log measure, with Gibrat growth plus entry and exit. d_log ≈ 1, with a small bottom-heavy correction set by entrant job flux / (total employment × log growth rate).
catalogue.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 is correct. The receipts decomposition gives c = 1.059/0.994 − 1 ≈ 0.065, but both SEs are about 0.06, so c = 0.07 ± 0.09, consistent with 0. The decomposition is not identified.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for the workers reading. The correction ζ − 1 = 0.06 is about one SE from 0, so the rate reading (m·τ ≈ 17) is not yet constrained. The receipts decomposition, with c backed out and indistinguishable from 0, is at best suggestive and closer to numerology.

proposed_readings.resource: Workers under proportional growth with entry and exit
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 + φ/m, where ζ − 1 ≈ J_R/(Q·m): annual employment created by entrants as a fraction of total employment, divided by the employment-weighted log growth rate. ζ − 1 = 0.059 implies m·τ_res ≈ 17.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Panel data (BDS-type) giving the entrant employment share and growth rates should predict ζ − 1 ≈ 0.06 out of sample. Periods of high entry should show steeper tails.

proposed_readings.resource: Receipts = workers × revenue per worker
proposed_readings.composition: If receipts R ∝ L^(1+c) deterministically, then ζ_R = ζ_L/(1+c). Receipts ζ ≈ 0.99 against employees ζ = 1.059 implies c ≈ 0.07.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: Elasticity of revenue per worker to firm size ≈ 0.07
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: A cross-sectional regression of ln(receipts/employee) on ln(employees) should give about 0.07. Large scatter at fixed size would break the deterministic map.

catalogue.system: Growth-rate volatility of firms (US publicly traded manufacturing firms, Compustat 1975–1991; pharmaceutical firms by product)
catalogue.law: σ(g | S) ∝ S^(−β): standard deviation of the annual log growth rate g at firm size S
catalogue.variable: S = sales (also employees, assets)
catalogue.reported: β = 0.20 ± 0.03 over about seven orders of magnitude of sales (Stanley et al. 1996 Nature, as restated by a 2017 re-analysis and arXiv 2404.15226). β = 0.14–0.2 depending on the average number of units per firm (Riccaboni et al. 2008 PNAS). Pure diversification over independent equal units would give 0.5.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: This field holds −β, a scaling exponent, not a density exponent. Stanley et al. 1996 (Nature) give β ≈ 0.15 ± 0.03 on Compustat 1974–1993. Amaral et al. 1997 (J. Phys. I), on the same database, give 0.20 ± 0.03 for sales and 0.18 ± 0.03 for employees and assets (recollection). The catalogue's '0.20 ± 0.03, Stanley 1996, 1975–1991' merges the two papers. Across papers β ranges 0.14–0.20.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the firm's absolute growth variance, which is additive over independent components. Units: effectively independent sub-units (products, divisions, plants). Resource per unit: each unit's variance, ∝ (unit size)². With n_eff ∝ S^0.4 units, each of size S/n_eff ∝ S^0.6, total variance ∝ S^0.4 × (S^0.6)² = S^1.6. The firm is a container whose size is shared among a slowly growing number of units, and β is half the exponent of that unit count.
catalogue.best_reading: Absolute growth variance is additive over effectively independent sub-units. The firm's size is spread over n_eff ∝ S^(0.3–0.4) units of size S^(0.6–0.7). Wyart & Bouchaud (2003), Sutton (2002) and Riccaboni et al. (2008) all derive this reading.
catalogue.algebra_note: Var(ΔS) = σ²S² ∝ S^(2−2β). Define n_eff = S²/ΣS_i². Then n_eff·(S/n_eff)² = S²/n_eff exactly, so n_eff ∝ S^(2β). The catalogue's 1.6 = 0.4 + 2×0.6 is correct for β = 0.2; β = 0.15 gives 1.7 = 0.3 + 1.4. Wyart–Bouchaud's β = 1 − 1/μ gives μ ≈ 1.18–1.25.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for the reading: additivity of variance is forced by statistics, and the decomposition is an identity once n_eff is defined by a Herfindahl index. The empirical content is n_eff ∝ S^(2β) measured at product level. Why 2β ≈ 0.3–0.4 has several competing derivations: Pareto sub-unit sizes, proportional growth of sub-units, and a hierarchical-tree model. So the reading is robust but the mechanism is not unique.

proposed_readings.resource: Absolute growth variance = (number of effective independent units) × (unit size)²
proposed_readings.composition: 2 − 2β = 2β + 2(1 − 2β), i.e. 1.6 = 0.4 + 2 × 0.6 (deterministic exponents add)
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: β = 1/2 if units are equal-sized and n ∝ S. β = 1 − 1/μ if unit sizes are Pareto with 1 < μ < 2 (Wyart & Bouchaud 2003, via a 2024 review); β = 0.2 then needs μ ≈ 1.25. Riccaboni et al. (2008): β crosses over from 0 for small firms to 1/2 for very large ones, staying at 0.14–0.2 for realistic numbers of units.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Within firms, the Herfindahl effective number of products (ΣS_i)²/ΣS_i² should scale as S^0.4. Under Wyart–Bouchaud, the product-size tail should have μ ≈ 1/(1−β) ≈ 1.25. β should rise toward 1/2 for the largest, most diversified firms.

catalogue.system: Richest US individuals (Forbes 400 lists, 1988–2003)
catalogue.law: P(W > w) ∝ w^-ζ in the top tail
catalogue.variable: w = net worth (US dollars)
catalogue.reported: ζ = 1.49, averaged over Forbes 400 lists 1988–2003 (Klass et al. 2006 Econ. Lett. 90:290). Other estimates on similar lists, 1.09–1.36 (Newman 2005; Levy & Solomon 1997), come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified. A fixed-k tail regression (arXiv 2105.10007) finds that top marginal income-tax rates of 30–40% correspond to ζ ≈ 1.5–1.8. The 80/20 rule corresponds to ζ = ln 5/ln 4 ≈ 1.16.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Klass et al. 2006 give an average ζ = 1.49 over the 1988–2003 lists (recollection; the repo agrees). The same kind of data gives other values: Levy & Solomon 1997, 1.36; Newman 2005, α = 2.09 (ζ = 1.09, x_min = $600M); Clauset 2009, α = 2.3 ± 0.1, with the pure power law rejected (p ≈ 0). So ζ ranges 1.1–1.5 by estimator and year. The fixed-k tax result (ζ 1.5–1.8) was not verified.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: wealth held by the top group (a stock). Units: persons or families. Resource: net worth. ζ ≈ 1.5 means wealth per log band falls as w^(−0.5) within the tail: bottom-heavy, with more total wealth near the entry threshold than among the very richest. Formally the log-orthopolic resource is w^1.5. The natural reading, though, is wealth itself plus a turnover correction of +0.5.
catalogue.best_reading: Wealth (q = k) under multiplicative returns with size-independent exit (Kesten/Gibrat). d_log = 1 plus a turnover correction that measured growth and exit rates should predict.
catalogue.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 is correct. One interpretation slip: from stationary resource accounting with deterministic growth m and size-independent exit rate δ, ζ = δ/m = 1 + J_R/(Q·m). So ζ − 1 = 0.49 means Q/J_R (resource turnover time via entry) ≈ 2/m. It does not mean a unit of wealth 'climbs about two e-folds before it leaves'. The mean climb before exit is m/δ = 1/ζ ≈ 0.67 e-folds.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low for the choice of resource. The 0.49 correction is backed out, and the ζ estimate itself spans 1.1–1.5, so the rate interpretation has not been tested. The w^1.5 liquidation-cost reading is numerology. The tax-direction evidence would be qualitative support, but I did not verify it here.

proposed_readings.resource: Wealth under multiplicative returns with exit (death, estate division, consumption, taxation, dropping off the list)
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 + φ/m ≈ 1 + 1/(m·τ_res). ζ − 1 = 0.49 implies m·τ_res ≈ 2: a unit of top wealth climbs only about two e-folds before it leaves the tail.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: ζ > 1, rising with turnover and taxation
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Taxation shortens residence and should raise ζ. The fixed-k tail regression finds ζ rising to 1.5–1.8 at 30–40% top rates, confirming the direction. A prediction from measured return dispersion and list turnover should reproduce ζ ≈ 1.5.

proposed_readings.resource: Liquidation cost under square-root market impact
proposed_readings.composition: w^1.5 = w × w^(1/2): wealth times the square-root price impact of selling it
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Would fix ζ at 1.5 regardless of taxation, which the observed tax dependence contradicts.

catalogue.system: US top personal incomes from IRS tabulations, 1916–2019, split into labor and capital income
catalogue.law: P(Y > y) ∝ y^-ζ in the top tail
catalogue.variable: y = annual income (US dollars per year), a flux
catalogue.reported: Labor income ζ ≈ 2 and capital income ζ ≈ 1.2, both stable since about 1985 (Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang 2022, arXiv 2206.04257, abstract). Total top income ζ ≈ 1.4–1.8 since 1985 (Toda & Wang, arXiv 1901.02471).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Labor ζ ≈ 2 and capital ζ ≈ 1.2, both stable for about three decades (abstract of Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang; recollection). Total top income ζ ≈ 1.4–1.8 (Toda & Wang) was not verified.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: income received by top earners per year (a flux). Units: taxpayers. Capital income is a flux drawn from a wealth stock (y_K = r·W) and inherits that stock's nearly log-orthopolic allocation (ζ ≈ 1.2). Labor income, with ζ ≈ 2, is far from orthopolic in itself. Its log-orthopolic quantity is y_L², i.e. labor income behaves like the square root of a Zipf-distributed stock.
catalogue.best_reading: For capital income: a flux r·W drawn from the near-Zipf wealth stock (motivated; that returns rise with wealth, ε > 0, is independently supported in direction by Fagereng et al. 2020 and Bach, Calvet & Sodini 2020; recollection). For labor income ζ ≈ 2, the exponent shown here, no reading rises above suggestive.
catalogue.algebra_note: ζ_y = ζ_S/κ and ζ_K = ζ_W/(1+ε) are correct. 1.49/1.2 − 1 ≈ 0.24 if the populations matched, but they do not (Forbes 400 versus IRS filers).
catalogue.numerology_risk: High for labor. At least two prior mechanisms fit ζ = 2 without fixing it. One is assignment to a Zipf-distributed scale with κ = 1/2, where κ is backed out from the exponent; only the CEO value κ = 1/3 is measured. The other is random earnings growth with exit or creative destruction (Jones & Kim 2018; Gabaix, Lasry, Lions & Moll 2016), which fits any ζ > 1. The y² reading is numerology. The CEO-pay ζ ≈ 3 prediction is a real out-of-sample test that has not been checked.

proposed_readings.resource: The size S of the organization or market an earner's talent is applied to (Zipf, ζ_S ≈ 1), with pay y ∝ S^κ
proposed_readings.composition: ζ_y = ζ_S/κ, so d_log(y) = 1/κ. Labor ζ ≈ 2 corresponds to κ ≈ 1/2. For CEOs, Roberts' law gives κ ≈ 1/3, so ζ_CEO pay ≈ 3.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: ζ_labor = 2 if κ = 1/2; ζ_CEO pay = 3 (my derivation from the Gabaix–Landier inputs)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: The CEO-pay tail should have ζ ≈ 3. Among top labor earners generally, the elasticity of pay to the scale they control should be about ζ_S/ζ_y ≈ 0.5.

proposed_readings.resource: Capital income as a flux: return × wealth stock
proposed_readings.composition: y_K = r·W with r ∝ W^ε gives ζ_K = ζ_W/(1+ε)
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: ζ_K = ζ_W ≈ 1.1–1.5 for size-independent returns; ζ_K < ζ_W if returns rise with wealth
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: The measured elasticity of realized returns to wealth, in one population, should equal ζ_W/ζ_K − 1.

proposed_readings.resource: Income squared
proposed_readings.composition: y² = y × y (e.g. a variance contribution)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: None

catalogue.system: Citations to scientific papers (ISI 1981 cohort, about 783,000 papers; Physical Review D volumes 11–50, 24,296 papers)
catalogue.law: N(x) ∝ x^-α in the high-citation tail, α ≈ 3
catalogue.variable: x = citations received per paper (count)
catalogue.reported: α ≈ 3, inferred from a rank slope of about 1/2 for top papers (Redner 1998 EPJ B 4:131). α = 3.16 ± 0.06 (Clauset et al. 2009) and 3.15 (Golosovsky & Solomon 2012) come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified here. Later work prefers double power laws (Lehmann et al.).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Redner 1998 gives α ≈ 3 (rank slope ≈ 1/2). Clauset 2009 gives 3.16 ± 0.06 at x_min = 160 (recollection; the repo agrees). Golosovsky & Solomon 2012 give ≈ 3.15. The power-law form is contested: field-normalized distributions collapse onto a lognormal (Radicchi, Fortunato & Castellano 2008), and Redner (2005) found a lognormal fits Physical Review data better.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the references made by citing papers. Each reference is one unit of credit, so the total is m times the number of citing papers. Units: cited papers. Resource per unit: citations received (a count of credit units, not a held stock). ζ = 2 means citations per log band fall as x^(−1): strongly bottom-heavy, with most credit going to moderately cited papers.
catalogue.best_reading: Relative age (exposure time) is exactly log-orthopolic because papers enter at a steady rate. Citations are a deterministic power of it, x ∝ u^θ with θ = m/(m+A), so d_log(x) = 1/θ = 2. The same structure underlies Simon's model (θ = 1 − a), the web (θ = m/(m+A)) and Lotka.
catalogue.algebra_note: γ = 2 + A/m is correct, so A = m gives 3. With steady arrival, P(t/t_i > u) = 1/u exactly, so the system is log-orthopolic in relative age u. x ∝ u^(m/(m+A)) = u^(1/2) then gives ζ_x = 2. The linear x³ reading only restates the log reading in another measure.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Medium. I downgraded the grade from 'derived'. The mechanism is prior (Price, DMS), but A = m is read off the exponent: Price's A ≈ 1 with m ≈ 20 references would give α ≈ 2.05. One prior argument for A = m exists: visibility proportional to total degree (k_in + m), as when papers are found by following links in both directions. It is not established. Aging and fitness (Wang, Song & Barabási 2013) change the tail, and lognormal alternatives fit.

proposed_readings.resource: Citations plus initial attractiveness under cumulative advantage (Price model; Dorogovtsev–Mendes–Samukhin)
proposed_readings.composition: d_log = 1 + A/m, i.e. ζ − 1 = A/m: the ratio of non-preferential attachment (initial attractiveness A) to preferential attachment per new paper carrying m references. α = 3 means A = m. Equivalently, in-degree grows as (t/t_i)^(m/(m+A)) = (t/t_i)^(1/2), and the system is log-orthopolic in relative age t/t_i ∝ x².
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: α = 2 + A/m; α = 3 when A = m (also the undirected Barabási–Albert value)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Measure the attachment kernel Π(x) ∝ x + A in a citation panel: A/m must equal α − 2 ≈ 1. Fields with more references per paper, at similar A, should have flatter tails.

proposed_readings.resource: Citations × relative age
proposed_readings.composition: x³ = x × x², under the linear measure
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: None independent

(2009); Dorogovtsev, Mendes & Samukhin (2000) PRL 85:4633; Radicchi, Fortunato & Castellano (2008) PNAS 105:17268. Recollection; web unavailable.

catalogue.system: Authors of scientific papers (Chemical Abstracts 1907–1916; Auerbach's physics index; later bibliographies)
catalogue.law: Lotka's law: y(n) ∝ n^-a, the number of authors with n papers, with a ≈ 2 (the 'inverse square law')
catalogue.variable: n = papers per author (count)
catalogue.reported: Lotka's least-squares slopes: 1.888 (Chemical Abstracts, senior authors only) and 2.021 (Auerbach) (via arXiv 1601.04950). The exponent varies by field and period; a 2026 sustainability-science study finds a higher exponent and prefers a lognormal. Clauset et al. 2009 report a MathSciNet tail α = 4.3 above n = 133 (repo compilation, from memory, not verified).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: Lotka 1926: 1.888 (Chemical Abstracts) and 2.021 (Auerbach), fitted over roughly n = 1 to 10–30 (recollection). The MathSciNet tail is α = 4.3 ± 0.1 above n = 133 (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo marks it as memory).
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: author–paper credits (each paper counted once per credited author). Units: authors. Resource per unit: papers. d_log ≈ 1 means each factor-of-ten productivity band (1–10 papers, 10–100 papers) contributes about the same number of papers.
catalogue.best_reading: Papers (q = k) under the log measure, with cumulative advantage and steady newcomer entry. d_log ≈ 1 holds only over the first decade of n.
catalogue.algebra_note: Recomputed: Lotka(2) truncated at n_max = 100–1000 gives mean productivity 3.17–4.55, a = 0.22–0.32, ζ = 1.28–1.46 and α = 2.28–2.46 (agrees). The Yule–Simon local slope for ρ = 1.28–1.46 is 1.92–2.03 over n = 1–10 and 2.23–2.39 over n = 10–100. The catalogue's '1.7–2.2' is too wide, and the true match to Lotka's values is closer than stated.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Medium-high. Over one decade almost any right-skewed distribution has a local slope near 2, and a lognormal (Shockley) fits comparably. The Simon asymptote (2.3–2.5) is contradicted by the MathSciNet tail (4.3), where finite careers dominate, so the mechanism fails exactly where it could be tested. The Shockley alternative is a counter-reading (no power law), suggestive.

proposed_readings.resource: Papers under cumulative advantage with newcomer entry (Simon/Price 'success breeds success')
proposed_readings.composition: d = 1 + a/(1−a), where a = share of papers by first-time authors = authors/papers. Lotka's own law truncated at n_max = 100–1000 implies mean productivity of 3.2–4.6, hence a ≈ 0.22–0.32 and ζ ≈ 1.28–1.46 (my computation).
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: Asymptotic tail α ≈ 2.3–2.5. The Yule–Simon local slope over n = 1–10 is 1.7–2.2 (my computation), matching the small-n range Lotka fitted.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Tails fitted above a theory-set n_min should be steeper than 2, by a/(1−a) computed from the same bibliography's authors/papers ratio. MathSciNet's steep tail points this way; finite careers would steepen it further.

proposed_readings.resource: Productivity as a product of independent personal factors (Shockley 1957)
proposed_readings.composition: Papers = Π f_i over several independent abilities, so log(papers) is a sum and the distribution is lognormal. Tail exponents of independent random factors do not add.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: A likelihood-ratio test of lognormal against power law on large bibliographies, with n_min fixed in advance

Wash. Acad. Sci. 16:317; Clauset et al. (2009); Simon (1955); Price (1976). Recollection; web unavailable.

catalogue.system: Journals contributing articles on a subject (Bradford's 1934 bibliographies and later subject bibliographies)
catalogue.law: Bradford's law, verbal form: ranked journals split into a core and zones that each yield the same number of articles, with journal counts in successive zones in the ratio 1 : n : n². Leimkuhler's form: cumulative articles F(x) = ln(1 + βx)/ln(1 + β).
catalogue.variable: k = relevant articles per journal; journals ranked r = 1, 2, … by productivity
catalogue.reported: The multiplier n is set empirically for each bibliography; there is no universal value. The verbal Bradford law, Leimkuhler's law and Lotka's law with exponent 2 are equivalent (Egghe 1988; Chen & Leimkuhler); the graphical form differs (Egghe). Real bibliographies deviate, and a 2021 polymer bibliography fails the verbal law but fits Leimkuhler.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: The verbal law is exact by construction. The empirical multiplier n is set per bibliography. Bradford's geophysics data were roughly 9 : 59 : 258 journals giving 429 : 499 : 404 articles (approximate recollection). The Groos droop is a common deviation.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the articles on the subject. Units: journals. Resource per unit: relevant articles. Bradford's verbal law is literally discrete orthopolity: the resource (articles) is equal per class, where the classes are geometric bands of journal rank, so articles are equal per log rank. It is the bibliometric statement of log-orthopolity with d = 1.
catalogue.best_reading: Discrete log-orthopolity of articles over geometric rank zones. Bradford's verbal law is itself the orthopolic statement with d = 1. Egghe proved it equivalent to Lotka(2) and Zipf(1).
catalogue.algebra_note: Equal articles per geometric zone gives cumulative articles ∝ ln r, so articles per journal ∝ 1/r, ζ = 1 and α = 2. The zone-yield ratio n^(1−1/ζ) is correct; 5^(1−1/1.1) = 1.158 (recomputed).
catalogue.numerology_risk: No freedom in the resource, but there are three caveats. First, it is not independent evidence: it is equivalent to Lotka(2)/Zipf(1) for the same data and should not be counted as a separate confirmation. Second, analysts choose the number of zones and the equal-yield boundaries and then report n, so the testable content is only the constancy of the zone multipliers. Third, the Groos droop and core curvature are frequent failures.

proposed_readings.resource: Articles per journal, discretely orthopolic over geometric rank zones
proposed_readings.composition: Zone j spans ranks n^j to n^(j+1). With articles per journal ∝ r^(−1/ζ), articles in zone j ∝ n^(j(1 − 1/ζ)), so equal yields across zones hold if and only if ζ = 1.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: Equal articles per zone; the ratio of successive zone yields is n^(1 − 1/ζ)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: If new journals keep entering (ζ = 1.1), then with n = 5 each zone should hold about 16% more articles than the previous one (5^(1 − 1/1.1) ≈ 1.16, my arithmetic). A Groos droop (fewer articles in the outer zones) points the other way, toward a lower cutoff or incomplete coverage.

Documentation 44:53; Leimkuhler (1967). Recollection; web unavailable.

catalogue.system: World Wide Web pages (AltaVista crawls of 1999, over 200 million pages and 1.5 billion links; nd.edu domain 1999)
catalogue.law: P(k_in) ∝ k_in^(−γ_in) with γ_in ≈ 2.1; out-degree γ_out ≈ 2.45–2.7
catalogue.variable: k = in-links per page (count)
catalogue.reported: γ_in = 2.1 (Broder et al. 2000, agreeing with earlier studies at smaller scales; Newman's 2001 review cites τ_in = 2.1). γ_out ≈ 2.7 for the AltaVista crawl (Broder et al., via Newman's review) and 2.45 for nd.edu (Albert, Jeong & Barabási 1999). Clauset et al. 2009 reject a pure power law for in-links (repo compilation, not re-verified).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: 2.1 is the published full-range in-degree value (Broder et al.; Albert et al.); out-degree is 2.72 (Broder) or 2.45 (nd.edu). A tail MLE gives α = 2.336 ± 0.009 at x_min = 3,684 with the pure power law rejected (p ≈ 0) (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo marks this as tentative). So α = 2.1–2.34, d_log = 1.1–1.34 and A/m = 0.1–0.34.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: hyperlinks (total in-degree = total out-degree). Units: pages. Resource per page: links received, i.e. attention conferred by other authors (a count of credit units). d_log ≈ 1.1 means links are almost log-orthopolic: each factor-of-ten band of popularity receives about the same number of links, with a 10% bottom-heavy correction. Out-degree is chosen by the page's own author, so its exponent has no comparable reading.
catalogue.best_reading: In-links (q = k) under the log measure, with preferential attachment and small initial attractiveness. d_log ≈ 1.1–1.3, so links are nearly log-orthopolic.
catalogue.algebra_note: d_log = 1.1 and d_lin = 2.1 are correct, and γ = 2 + A/m is correct.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Medium. A/m is read off the exponent, and the exponent itself depends on x_min (2.1 versus 2.34). Measured attachment kernels in online networks are often sublinear (recollection, not verified), and a pure power law is rejected in the tail. For out-degree the right grade is 'none' (no reading), not 'numerology'. It is a genuine counterexample.

proposed_readings.resource: In-links under preferential attachment with initial attractiveness
proposed_readings.composition: d_log = 1 + A/m; γ = 2 + A/m, so A/m ≈ 0.1
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: The Web's measured attachment kernel should be nearly linear with offset A ≈ 0.1·m. Citations (A ≈ m) should differ from the Web (A ≈ 0.1·m) because direct search matters more for papers.

proposed_readings.resource: Out-links as authoring effort (same lens applied to out-degree)
proposed_readings.composition: No accepted proportional-growth mechanism exists for a page's own outgoing links. Any reading q ∝ k^1.7 would be built from the exponent itself.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: None. That absence is what makes this a counterexample.

catalogue.system: US stocks (every trade on NYSE, AMEX and Nasdaq, 1994–1995; 40 million data points), plus LSE and Paris for volume
catalogue.law: Inverse cubic law: P(|r| > x) ∝ x^(−ζ_r) with ζ_r ≈ 3. Half-cubic law for trading volume: P(V > v) ∝ v^(−3/2).
catalogue.variable: r = normalized price change (return) over short intervals; V = shares traded
catalogue.reported: ζ_r ≈ 3. Fits give 3.1 ± 0.03 (positive tail) and 2.84 ± 0.12 (negative tail) over 2–100 standard deviations; extrapolation gives 2.84 ± 0.12 and 2.73 ± 0.13, with tail labels inconsistent in the preprint (Gopikrishnan et al. 1998). Volume ζ_V ≈ 3/2 (Gopikrishnan et al. 2000; LSE, 262 stocks, ≈ 3/2, consistent with NYSE and Paris per Plerou et al. 2004).
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: ζ_r = 3.10 ± 0.03 (positive tail) and 2.84 ± 0.12 (negative tail) for about 1,000 US stocks, 1994–95, over 2–100 SD (recollection). ζ_V ≈ 1.5 (Gopikrishnan et al. 2000; Plerou & Stanley 2007 across NYSE, LSE and Paris). This is disputed: Rácz, Eisler & Kertész (2009) find volume exponents that differ by stock and are often higher. Return tails vary roughly 2–5 across markets and horizons.
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: Returns are not a resource. The orthopolic stock behind them is the assets S of the institutions whose trades move prices. Fund sizes are roughly Zipf (ζ_S ≈ 1), i.e. log-orthopolic in assets. The chain V ∝ S^(2/3) (optimal trade size) and r ∝ V^(1/2) (square-root impact) gives r ∝ S^(1/3), so the log-orthopolic resource written in the return coordinate is S ∝ r³, and d_log = 3. The cubic law says the assets behind a trade scale as the cube of the return it causes. The linear reading is equal contributions to the fourth moment per unit return, so kurtosis diverges.
catalogue.best_reading: The assets of trading institutions, a stock assumed to be Zipf, seen through the optimal trade size V ∝ S^(2/3) and square-root impact r ∝ V^(1/2). The log-orthopolic resource in the return coordinate is S ∝ r³ (Gabaix, Gopikrishnan, Plerou & Stanley 2003).
catalogue.algebra_note: V ∝ S^(1/(1+δ)) and r ∝ V^δ give ζ_V = ζ_S(1+δ) and ζ_r = ζ_S(1+δ)/δ. For δ = 1/2 these are 3/2 and 3. Correct.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Low-medium. The inputs are measured separately from returns, and square-root impact of metaorders is now well supported (Tóth et al. 2011; recollection). But fund sizes may be lognormal rather than Zipf (Schwarzkopf & Farmer 2010), and large returns are often driven by order-book gaps rather than large orders (Farmer et al. 2004). GARCH/Kesten also gives 3–4 with fitted parameters. A clean test: ζ_r/ζ_V = 1/δ across markets with different impact exponents.

proposed_readings.resource: Assets under management of the trading institution (a Zipf stock) seen through two deterministic maps
proposed_readings.composition: Nested maps multiply exponents: d_log(r) = ζ_S × (d ln S/d ln V) × (d ln V/d ln r) = 1 × 3/2 × 2 = 3, and d_log(V) = 1 × 3/2 = 3/2. With a general impact exponent δ, ζ_r = ζ_S(1+δ)/δ and ζ_V = ζ_S(1+δ) (my generalization of the chain).
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: ζ_r = 2ζ_V wherever impact is square-root, independent of the fund-size distribution. The LSE volume ζ_V ≈ 3/2 supports the volume link. Markets with a different impact exponent δ should show ζ_r/ζ_V = 1/δ. The theory also predicts a number-of-trades exponent of about 3.4 (not verified here).

proposed_readings.resource: Volatility as a multiplicatively reinvested stock (GARCH/Kesten)
proposed_readings.composition: σ²_t = ω + (a·z²_(t−1) + b)·σ²_(t−1); ζ solves E[(a·z² + b)^(ζ/2)] = 1
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: ζ ≈ 3–4 for typical fitted (a, b) (not verified here)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: ζ should vary with the fitted persistence a + b across assets and periods, whereas the fund-size reading ties it to ζ_V. Both readings currently fit.

catalogue.system: Interstate wars, Correlates of War 1823–2003 (95 wars)
catalogue.law: Richardson's law: P(x) ∝ x^(−α) for battle deaths x ≥ x_min
catalogue.variable: x = battle deaths per war
catalogue.reported: α = 1.53 ± 0.07 for x ≥ 7,061 (51 of 95 wars; p_KS = 0.78 ± 0.03) (Clauset 2018 Sci. Adv. and 2019 chapter, arXiv 1901.05086). Per-capita intensity α = 1.7 ± 0.2 (Clauset et al. 2009) and 1.80 (Newman 2005) come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: 1.53 ± 0.07 at x_min = 7,061, from 95 wars with 51 in the tail (Clauset 2018; recollection). Per-capita intensity gives α = 1.7 ± 0.2 (Clauset 2009) and 1.80 (Newman 2005).
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: An event total (deaths in one war), not a held stock. Conserved total: battle deaths over the observation window. Units: wars. ζ ≈ 0.5 means deaths per log band rise as x^0.47: strongly top-heavy, with the total dominated by the largest wars (WWII, 16.6 million). The log-orthopolic resource is about x^(1/2).
catalogue.best_reading: α = 3/2 is equivalent to ζ = 1/2, i.e. war severity is log-orthopolic in √x. Three mechanisms give exactly this: critical branching (log-orthopolic in duration, with x ∝ T²), constant-kernel coagulation, and stopped multiplicative escalation. The escalation (flux) reading has the most data behind it, but its exponent is a fitted rate ratio.
catalogue.algebra_note: d_log = 0.53 and ζ = 0.53 are correct. Mean-field branching gives sizes s^(−3/2) and durations T^(−2) with s ∝ T². The coagulation family gives ζ = (1+ν)/2. Both are correct. Because α < 2, the mean diverges.
catalogue.numerology_risk: High. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated': at least three simple mechanisms give 3/2, so matching 1.53 does not tell them apart. The branching reading fails its own test, because durations are not T^(−2). With α < 2 the total is dominated by the largest war (WWII), so the 'conserved total' does not average out. The escalation paper (arXiv 2503.03945) could not be verified here.

proposed_readings.resource: War duration (generations of escalation) in a critical branching cascade
proposed_readings.composition: Mean-field critical branching gives P(T) ∝ T^(−2) (ζ_T = 1, i.e. log-orthopolic in duration) and size s ∝ T², hence α_s = 3/2. The resource is T ∝ s^(1/2).
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: War durations should follow P(T) ∝ T^(−2), with deaths ∝ duration². Instead 79% of wars end within two years, and civil wars last longer while being smaller, which does not support it.

proposed_readings.resource: Coalition mass under source-driven coagulation with a constant kernel (ν = 0)
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: The same family gives ζ = 1 for ν = 1 and 3/2 for ν = 2. ν would have to be measured from how conflicts merge.

proposed_readings.resource: Severity under year-to-year multiplicative escalation, stopped at random ('killed' multiplicative growth)
proposed_readings.composition: Transport identity with growth outpacing termination: ζ − 1 = φ/m < 0. ζ ≈ 0.5 means the log-growth of severity dominates exit, giving a top-heavy allocation; the exponent is a rate ratio, not a dimension.
proposed_readings.predicted_exponent: α between 1 and 2, set by the distribution of escalation factors and the hazard of ending
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Civil wars, which de-escalate once large, should have steeper tails than interstate wars; this is reported qualitatively. Per-capita normalization changes α (1.53 → 1.7), so the resource definition must be fixed in advance.

catalogue.system: Terrorist attacks worldwide (MIPT database 1968–2006, about 9,000 events); insurgent attacks in Iraq, Colombia, Afghanistan and other conflicts
catalogue.law: P(x) ∝ x^(−α) for deaths per attack, x ≥ x_min
catalogue.variable: x = deaths per attack
catalogue.reported: MLE α ≈ 2.4. In this task this was confirmed only through Mohler's published discussion of Clauset & Woodard 2013, which also notes bootstrap estimates clustering near 2.2. The Clauset et al. 2009 table value 2.4 ± 0.2 at x_min = 12 comes from the repo compilation. Insurgent-event size exponents cluster around 2.5, and extensions span 1.9–4.5 (as stated in a later paper citing Bohorquez et al. 2009 and Johnson et al. 2013). Lognormal and stretched-exponential fits are also plausible.
catalogue.alpha_uncertainty: 2.4 ± 0.2 at x_min = 12 ± 4 with p = 0.68 (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo agrees). Clauset, Young & Gleditsch (2007) give ≈ 2.38, and insurgencies give ≈ 2.5 (Johnson et al. 2006; Bohorquez et al. 2009).
catalogue.orthopolic_reading: An event total. Units: attacks. ζ ≈ 1.4 means deaths per log band fall as x^(−0.4): bottom-heavy, so most deaths come from small and medium attacks, unlike interstate wars. The log-orthopolic resource is x^1.4–1.5.
catalogue.best_reading: Coalescence–fragmentation of attack units. The final resource is members × merger log-speed = s^(3/2), with deaths assumed proportional to unit size.
catalogue.algebra_note: n_s ∝ s^(−(3+ν)/2), so ν = 2 gives 5/2. Then B = s²n ∝ s^((1−ν)/2) and v ∝ s^((ν−1)/2) = s^(1/2), so q = members × merger log-speed = s^(3/2) and d_log = 1.5. Verified. 'Deaths ∝ unit size' adds a deterministic map whose exponent is assumed to be 1.
catalogue.numerology_risk: Medium-high. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated'. Within 2.4 ± 0.2, 5/2 fits, but so does Gibrat with entry (any α > 2) and a lognormal. The deaths ∝ size map is untested. The model family was later tuned to cover α ≈ 1.9–4.5, so 5/2 is not a sharp prediction. Grading this ζ = (1+ν)/2 family 'motivated' here and 'numerology' for wars is inconsistent unless ν is measured in both.

proposed_readings.resource: Attack-unit size under coalescence–fragmentation with size-proportional merging
proposed_readings.composition: A mean-field merging rate ∝ s_i·s_j (kernel homogeneity ν = 2) gives group sizes n_s ∝ s^(−5/2). Transport reading: a constant member flux through sizes divided by the log-speed v ∝ s^((ν−1)/2) = s^(1/2), so d_log = 1 (members) + 1/2 (merger log-speed) = 3/2. Deaths are assumed ∝ unit strength.
proposed_readings.testable_consequence: Where group sizes can be observed, they should show density exponent 5/2. Within the same family, the contrast with wars (ν = 0, giving 3/2) requires interstate coalitions to merge at size-independent rates, which can be checked.
